Kraus WE.lab_name: Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and Division of Cardiology, Duke University School of Medicine (Durham, North Carolina, USA)
Kraus WE.role: Preventive cardiologist and exercise physiologist at Duke University who leads long-running trials on how exercise and calorie restriction change human health, and senior author of the CALERIE two-year safety report
Kraus WE.sub: Richard and Pat Johnson University Distinguished Professor, Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Duke University School of Medicine (since 2017) · Professor of Medicine (since 2006) · Duke Molecular Physiology Institute (since 2013) · MD, Duke University (1982)
story: Calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, slows aging in many animals and lowers mTOR activity. CALERIE (Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy) was the first long trial to test it in healthy, non-obese people. William Kraus is last author of the 2016 report on its safety (ROM2016). Over two years, participants aimed to eat 25% fewer calories. The diet was safe overall, with no rise in serious problems, but bone density fell more than in the control group, so bone health needs watching in anyone who tries long-term restriction.

Kraus earned an MD at Duke University in 1982 and trained as an internist and preventive cardiologist, a heart doctor who focuses on stopping disease before it starts. Kraus has been Professor of Medicine at Duke since 2006 and Richard and Pat Johnson University Distinguished Professor since 2017, and is a member of the Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and a professor in the School of Nursing. The group combines studies in people with lab work. It asks how exercise changes the body in healthy people, in people at risk such as those with pre-diabetes, and in people with heart disease or heart failure. It also looks for genes that raise the risk of early heart disease and metabolic syndrome, and studies how signals inside skeletal muscle adapt to exercise, heart failure, aging and spaceflight.

Kraus's PubMed record runs to hundreds of papers from Duke on exercise, heart and metabolic health. A 2026 follow-up of STRRIDE, a supervised exercise trial, found that step counts from wearable devices tracked fitness and heart-health measures better than people's own reports of how much they exercised.

Hakkola J.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Hakkola J.role: Professor of Pharmacology at the University of Oulu who studies the pregnane X receptor (PXR), a liver sensor of drugs and foreign chemicals, and how it changes liver growth and metabolism
Hakkola J.sub: Professor of Pharmacology (since 2009) and Head of the Research Unit of Biomedicine (since 2014), Faculty of Medicine, University of Oulu · Biocenter Oulu and Medical Research Center Oulu
story: Jukka Hakkola is the senior author of LASSILA2026, a study that joins a small clinical trial with mouse work. The pregnane X receptor (PXR) is a protein in liver cells that detects many drugs and chemicals and switches on genes to deal with them. Rifampicin, an antibiotic, activates it strongly. In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin made the liver about 2.7 percent larger relative to body weight. In male mice, activating PXR also enlarged the liver, and this came with higher activity of the AKT-MTOR growth pathway but not of YAP, another known driver of liver growth. The human part shows the effect is real in people, while the mTOR link comes from the mice.

Hakkola has worked on PXR for many years. PubMed lists him on more than 25 PXR papers from the University of Oulu, usually as senior author. A 2025 study from the group, for example, found Lasp2, a small cell-adhesion protein, as a new PXR target gene in mouse liver, with partners at Charles University in Hradec Kralove, Czech Republic. The wider theme is how drug-sensing receptors in the liver also change glucose and fat metabolism and the size of the organ.

Hakkola, who holds an MD and a PhD, has been Professor of Pharmacology at the University of Oulu since 2009 and head of its Research Unit of Biomedicine since 2014. The team works on nuclear receptors, proteins that switch genes on when they bind a signal molecule, and on cytochrome P450 enzymes, which break down drugs in the liver. Its main current target is PXR and how it shapes glucose and fat metabolism and metabolic disease. Other topics include sirtuins, PGC-1alpha and vitamin D metabolism.

Kim DJ.lab_name: Denali Therapeutics (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Kim DJ.role: Structural biologist, now at Denali Therapeutics, who worked in James Hurley's lab at UC Berkeley on the protein machines of autophagy and on the Rag-Ragulator complex that brings mTORC1 to the lysosome
Kim DJ.sub: Denali Therapeutics, South San Francisco (Hurley lab alumni list) · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences, University of California, Berkeley (Hurley lab, papers 2014–2019)
story: Do Jin Kim is a co-author of three Berkeley papers in this Atlas that describe, in atomic detail, the docking station for mTORC1, the growth-control complex, on the lysosome. SUX2017 combined several structural methods into a 'hybrid' model of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex, the scaffold that holds the Rag GTPases on the lysosome surface. LAW2018 found that nutrients change how tightly the Rag GTPases bind their lysosomal scaffold, Ragulator, a switch that controls whether mTORC1 is pulled to the lysosome. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited. Loss of FLCN causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition with kidney tumours.
Structures like these explain how a nutrient signal is turned into a physical change in proteins, and they show where drugs might act. They come from purified proteins and cells, not from animals.

Kim's earlier papers with Hurley's group, from 2014 and 2015, mapped the protein complexes that start autophagy: the Atg1/ULK1 complex, the autophagy PI3-kinase complex and the Atg13-Atg101 pair. The Hurley lab's alumni list now places Kim at Denali Therapeutics, a biotechnology company in South San Francisco. It does not give a job title.

Covey DF.lab_name: Department of Developmental Biology and Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research, Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, Missouri, USA)
Covey DF.role: Medicinal chemist and Andrew C and Barbara B Taylor Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry at Washington University in St. Louis who designs synthetic steroids and sterols to study neurosteroids, GABA-A receptors and cholesterol sensing, including in two Atlas studies on cholesterol and mTORC1
Covey DF.sub: Andrew C and Barbara B Taylor Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry · Professor of Developmental Biology, of Anesthesiology and of Psychiatry, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis · Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research
story: Douglas Covey is a co-author of two Atlas studies from the Zoncu lab on how lysosomes tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that cholesterol is available. In CAS2017 the team showed that cholesterol in the lysosome membrane switches on mTORC1. The transporter SLC38A9 is needed for this through cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein, separate from its role in sensing arginine, while NPC1, the protein that exports cholesterol out of the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. In SHI2022 they found a second sensor, LYCHOS (formerly called GPR155). When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS binds GATOR1, a brake on mTORC1, and takes it out of action, so mTORC1 can be recruited to the lysosome. Both studies were done mainly in cultured cells.

Covey's own field is the chemistry of steroids and sterols. Covey's group at Washington University makes modified versions of these molecules and tests how small changes in shape alter what they do. Much of this work, often with Mennerick, concerns neurosteroids, natural brain steroids that act on GABA-A receptors, the main inhibitory receptors of the brain, and their potential for treating psychiatric disorders. Recent papers use machine learning and screening to find new neurosteroid targets (2025), test steroid and sterol analogues on inflammation in brain immune cells (2026) and show that flipping the orientation of one hydroxy group in cholesterol changes how the molecule moves inside cells (2026).

Covey holds the Andrew C and Barbara B Taylor Distinguished Professorship of Psychiatry at Washington University School of Medicine, together with professorships in developmental biology, anesthesiology and psychiatry. PubMed also lists the Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research. In September 2026 the Department of Developmental Biology held a half-day symposium named after Covey.

Davis OB.lab_name: Zoncu Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Davis OB.role: Cell biologist who did a PhD in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley on how lysosomal cholesterol controls mTORC1, and first author of a 2020 study proposing NPC1-mTORC1 signalling as a drug target in Niemann-Pick type C disease
Davis OB.sub: PhD, University of California, Berkeley (2020, advisor Roberto Zoncu) · Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and Paul F. Glenn Center for Aging Research, University of California, Berkeley (Zoncu lab, papers 2017–2022, at the time of the study)
story: Oliver Davis is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas on cholesterol and mTORC1. Every cell has to decide whether it has enough raw materials to grow. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, makes that decision on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, where it is switched on when nutrients are present. Amino acids were the best-known signal; CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is another one. SLC38A9, a transporter-like protein already known to sense the amino acid arginine, is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and it uses separate cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein to do it. NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The experiments used cell lines and fibroblasts from patients, not whole animals. SHI2022 then found the cholesterol sensor itself: LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein previously known only as GPR155. Cholesterol binds one end of LYCHOS, and when cholesterol is high LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that normally keeps mTORC1 off, which lets mTORC1 be recruited to the lysosome. This work was done in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Davis followed this up as first author of a 2020 Developmental Cell paper titled 'NPC1-mTORC1 signaling couples cholesterol sensing to organelle homeostasis and is a targetable pathway in Niemann-Pick type C'. Niemann-Pick type C is a rare inherited disease in which cholesterol gets trapped in lysosomes and the brain and liver are damaged. The paper linked this cholesterol signal to the health of the cell's organelles and suggested that blocking mTORC1 could be a way to treat the disease. Davis was also second author of a 2019 Nature Cell Biology paper showing that contacts between the endoplasmic reticulum and the lysosome let mTORC1 sense cholesterol and drive abnormal growth signalling in the same disease.

Davis completed a PhD dissertation at UC Berkeley in 2020 with Roberto Zoncu as advisor, titled 'The Role of Lysosomal Cholesterol Transport in Cellular Nutrient Sensing and Organelle Homeostasis'. It gathers the cholesterol and mTORC1 work described above. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

Gnant M.lab_name: Department of Surgery and Comprehensive Cancer Center, Medical University of Vienna (Vienna, Austria)
Gnant M.role: Surgical oncologist and breast cancer trialist, Professor of Surgery at the Medical University of Vienna and President of the Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group, and a co-author of BOLERO-2, the trial that brought the mTOR inhibitor everolimus into breast cancer treatment
Gnant M.sub: Professor of Surgery, Medical University of Vienna · President, Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group (since 2005) · Professor of Surgical Oncology, Medical University of Vienna (2004) · Associate Professor of Surgery, University of Vienna (2000) · Visiting Scientist, National Cancer Institute, Bethesda (1997)
story: Most breast cancers grow in response to the hormone estrogen, and hormone therapy is the main treatment. Over time many tumours stop responding, and part of that resistance runs through mTOR. BOLERO-2 (BAS2012) was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women whose hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor. Adding the mTOR inhibitor everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, 10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review. The result led to approval of the combination. Mouth sores (stomatitis) were the main side effect. Michael Gnant was one of the co-authors.

The final overall-survival report (PIC2014) found a median of 31.0 months with everolimus plus exemestane and 26.6 months with placebo plus exemestane. That gap was not statistically significant, so the drug delayed progression but was not shown to lengthen life. Both papers are human trials.

Gnant is Professor of Surgery at the Medical University of Vienna and has led the Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group (ABCSG), the national cancer trials group, as President since 2005. After a period as a visiting scientist at the US National Cancer Institute in Bethesda in 1997, Gnant became associate professor of surgery at the University of Vienna in 2000 and professor of surgical oncology at the Medical University of Vienna in 2004. The research covers hormone therapy for breast cancer, CDK4/6 inhibitors, treatments that protect bone during cancer therapy and the design of large clinical trials, with earlier work on pancreatic cancer. Gnant was elected to Academia Europaea in 2025. PubMed lists close to 100 papers with Gnant, Vienna and ABCSG, such as a 2026 Austrian consensus on CDK4/6 inhibitors after surgery for early breast cancer.

Paul D.lab_name: Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Paul D.role: Postdoctoral fellow in Steven Cappell's lab at the National Cancer Institute who studies how ubiquitin ligases time the start of the cell cycle, and who found that mTOR briefly switches off the APC/C to give cells a burst of glycolysis as they start to divide
Paul D.sub: Postdoctoral fellow, Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (papers 2021–2025) · PhD on ubiquitin ligases
story: Debasish Paul is first author of PAU2025, a Nature paper about the moment a resting cell decides to divide. When a growth signal arrives, mTOR quickly adds a phosphate to CDH1, the helper protein of a large enzyme called APC/C that tags other proteins for destruction. This partly releases CDH1 and briefly switches APC/C off. One of APC/C's usual targets, the glycolysis enzyme PFKFB3, then builds up, and the cell burns more glucose for a while, until a slower-acting phosphatase turns APC/C back on. The study, in human cells, showed that this short pulse of glycolysis is needed for cells to enter the cell cycle.

The finding gives mTOR a new job: besides boosting protein synthesis, it times a metabolic switch by reaching into the cell-cycle machinery. Because many cancers have overactive mTOR, the circuit may also help explain how tumor cells keep their fuel supply high, although the paper itself did not test tumors.

Paul is a postdoctoral fellow in Steven Cappell's lab at the Center for Cancer Research of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda, and the publication record places Paul there from at least 2021. That year the group showed that cells hit by DNA damage early in the cycle often keep going rather than stopping at the classic checkpoint. The lab uses time-lapse imaging of single living cells to follow cell-cycle decisions.

Paul's PhD was on ubiquitin ligases, enzymes that tag other proteins with a small protein called ubiquitin, often marking them for destruction. In the Cappell lab Paul studies how the activity of these enzymes rises and falls as a resting cell re-enters the cell cycle, focusing on the APC/C, and is building fluorescent biosensors that report ubiquitin ligase activity in living cells.

Shimada H.lab_name: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Shimada H.role: Obstetrician-scientist from Sapporo Medical University working in the Colorado placenta group of Thomas Jansson, Theresa Powell and Fredrick Rosario on how mTOR controls nutrient transport to the fetus
Shimada H.sub: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (2024–2026) · Visiting researcher, Faculty of Medicine, Sapporo Medical University (2020, 2026) · Researcher, Faculty of Medicine, Sapporo Medical University (2019)
story: The placenta decides how much food reaches a growing baby, and mTORC1, the cell's nutrient and growth sensor, helps set how fast it pumps amino acids across. In the 2026 study led by Hiroshi Shimada, with Fredrick Rosario as senior author, the team compared 46 placentas from healthy term pregnancies. Placentas from boys showed stronger mTORC1 signalling, more System A amino acid transport and higher mitochondrial respiration than placentas from girls, and boys had a higher birth weight relative to placental weight.

This was a snapshot at one time point with no treatment, so it shows an association between fetal sex and placental function, not a cause. It does suggest that male and female pregnancies may need to be analysed separately in placental research.

Shimada is listed by PubMed with both the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Sapporo Medical University in Japan. Earlier work in the Colorado group includes a 2024 review on how placental amino acid transporters are regulated, with mTOR as a key regulator, and a 2025 mouse study in which switching off mTOR only in placental trophoblast cells cut the transport of folate to the fetus and reduced fetal growth.

The Japanese national research database KAKEN lists Shimada at the Faculty of Medicine of Sapporo Medical University, as a researcher in 2019 and as a visiting researcher in 2020 and 2026, in the field of obstetrics and gynecology. There Shimada led an early-career grant from 2019 to 2020 to study how endometriosis, the growth of womb-lining tissue outside the womb, develops, using a new disease model.
